Eyal's stronger move is not a sermon about avoiding all peers. It is teaching children to build social antibodies so their friendships can protect attention instead of quietly draining it.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 29 asks what happens when a child's growing commitments meet other children. The answer is not as simple as 'ignore peer pressure.' Friends are part of the environment, and other people can act like external triggers too. A group chat, a lunch table norm, a joking invitation, or a shared habit can keep distraction moving through a group long after one child has started trying to own their choices.

That is why the chapter uses the language of social antibodies. The point is not to make the child socially brittle or suspicious of every friend. The point is to help them build social responses, group expectations, and small protective norms that keep attention from collapsing the moment company arrives.

The chapter matters because self-authored pacts from Chapter 28 will stay thin if they only work in solitude. A child who can keep one promise alone but loses it the second friends enter the scene still has a social weak point that needs attention.

The chapter also avoids a cliche. It is not merely telling children to be morally heroic against bad peers. It is asking how peer culture itself can be shaped so focused behavior, honest exits, and mutual protection become more normal.

That is what keeps the chapter developmental and humane. Children are social learners. The right move is not to pretend friendship does not matter. It is to help them make friendship less hostile to what matters.

That makes the final chapter's bridge clear. Once distraction is seen as relational and contagious among friends, the book can close by widening that insight into adult intimacy and love.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 29 argues that peer norms can spread distraction or help resist it. Friends are not outside the system. They are part of the environment, and other people can function as external triggers.

This matters because a child-owned pact that works only in private is not yet socially durable. Group chats, jokes, pressure, and friend habits can undo a commitment unless the child has social antibodies ready.

Those antibodies are not grand speeches. They are practical social protections: honest phrases, agreed norms, exit moves, and friendships where focus is not mocked on sight.

The chapter also avoids reducing everything to bad-friend morality. The stronger move is to shape peer culture so healthier norms become easier to live inside.

That is why the final chapter can widen the frame from children among friends to adults in love. Attention has been social all along.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 29 says the playground has a constitution whether adults acknowledge it or not. Every friend group teaches what is normal to click, answer, laugh at, delay, or ditch. That means distraction is not only personal weakness. It can become a group habit that keeps reproducing itself through jokes, expectations, and tiny bids for reaction.

That is why this chapter rejects the lazy advice to simply 'stand strong.' Lone bravery matters, but it will keep bleeding if the social weather stays hostile. Eyal's stronger move is social antibodies: prepared lines, shared agreements, friendly refusals, and peer norms that make attention easier to keep in public.

This matters because Chapter 28's promises are now walking into the crowd. A pact with fingerprints on it still needs a social immune system.

The chapter also keeps its dignity by refusing cheap anti-peer-pressure melodrama. Children do not need a lecture that treats every friend as corruption. They need help seeing how cultures form and how cultures can be nudged.

That prepares the closing chapter perfectly. Once you admit attention is vulnerable to the people around you, love stops looking like a separate topic and starts looking like the deepest relational test of the whole book.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 29 asks what becomes of a child's growing self-control once other children enter the scene. The answer is not that the earlier work disappears. It is that the earlier work meets a new layer of pressure. Friends are part of the environment, and other people can operate as external triggers just as surely as devices, rooms, and routines can.

That matters because children do not merely occupy social settings. They are trained by them. A joke can normalize drift. A group chat can reward instant reaction. A lunch-table expectation can make delay feel like social risk. A self-authored pact from the prior chapter may be sincere and still buckle under that kind of ambient pressure.

That is why the chapter turns toward social antibodies. The term matters because the solution is not a lonely speech about character. The child needs workable social protections: phrases they can use without sounding absurd, agreements that friends can recognize, exit moves that preserve dignity, and peer cultures where focus is not treated like betrayal.

The chapter also protects itself from cliche. It does not treat peers as villains or tell the reader to solve the issue through isolation. Children are social learners and friendship is not the enemy. The stronger move is to notice how norms form and then make better norms easier to inhabit.

This is where the earlier parts of the book quietly converge. Internal triggers still matter because social risk feels uncomfortable. Time for traction still matters because children need to know what they are protecting. External-trigger logic still matters because other people are part of the cue system. Pacts still matter because social life tests whether a promise can survive contact.

That is why the chapter functions as more than a child-behavior appendix. It shows that attention is already social. The final chapter only carries that truth deeper into adult intimacy, where repeated partial attention can wound a bond without ever looking dramatic from the outside.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 29 says peer culture is not background noise. It is one of the places where distraction gets copied, rewarded, and normalized. Friends can act as external triggers, and group norms can quietly make reaction feel more urgent than intention.

That is why the chapter introduces social antibodies. The child does not just need private resolve. They need social protections that work in the real company they keep: phrases, agreements, exits, and norms that lower the social cost of staying aligned with what matters.

This matters because Chapter 28's self-authored pacts are being stress-tested here. A promise that works only in solitude has not yet survived the crowd.

The chapter also avoids cheap peer-pressure drama. The point is not to divide the world into pure children and bad friends. The point is to shape cultures where healthier behavior becomes easier to practice together.

That makes the closing move of the book feel earned. Once attention is understood as something friendship can either protect or tax, love becomes the final, deepest relational test.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 29 says stop pretending the crowd is scenery. The crowd is software. It teaches defaults, punishes hesitation, rewards instant response, and decides what kinds of delay feel embarrassing. That means a child's distraction problem can be partly social even when nobody around them looks malicious.

So the book does not ask for one more heroic speech about backbone. It asks for social antibodies: live phrases, visible agreements, honorable exits, and friend norms that keep the promise from dying the second the group starts laughing.

This is the real exam for Chapter 28. A pact with fingerprints on it still needs an immune system when the playground starts passing around a virus.

The chapter keeps its intelligence by refusing isolation fantasy. Friendship is not the contaminant. Unexamined norms are. The job is to build better weather, not to ban the sky.

That is exactly why the closing chapter works. Once you see that attention is something other people can either erode or protect, intimacy stops being sentimental side content. It becomes the room where the bill is highest.
